docs.title: 12. Chat channels and agent-to-agent talk
docs.text:
Added in 0.7.1 (myclaw/chat/, myclaw/events.py, myclaw/web/chat_api.py, webui/src/components/ChatView.tsx).

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as You
    participant UI as Chat (React)
    participant WS as /ws/channels/{id}
    participant E as ChatEngine
    participant S as chat.db
    participant A1 as @default
    participant A2 as @writer
    participant EV as events.py

    U->>UI: "@default ask writer for a haiku"
    UI->>WS: {type: message}
    WS->>E: post()
    E->>S: save your message
    E->>E: who answers? @mentions, else reply mode<br/>(lead · everyone in turn · everyone at once)
    E->>A1: stream_think(group context + message)<br/>CURRENT_CHANNEL / CURRENT_AGENT set
    A1->>EV: delegation_start (default → writer)
    EV-->>WS: event → card in chat + Activity panel
    EV->>S: saved as an "event" message
    A1->>A2: delegate tool → think(task)
    A2-->>A1: haiku
    A1->>EV: delegation_end (+ result, ms)
    A1-->>E: answer tokens
    E-->>WS: stream_start · chunk… · stream_end (model, time)
    E->>S: save the answer
  • Each (channel, agent) pair has its own conversation memory (MEMORY_SCOPE); the knowledge base is shared.
  • Tool calls (tool_start / tool_end), swarm hand-offs and job runs travel the same way. Nothing is emitted when no channel is set, so the CLI, Telegram and tests are unaffected.

docs.title: 13. Jobs
docs.text:
Added in 0.7.1 (myclaw/jobs/, myclaw/web/jobs_api.py, Jobs page).

flowchart LR
    ui["Jobs page / API<br/>add · edit · pause · run now"] --> store[("jobs.db<br/>jobs + runs")]
    tick["runner loop<br/>(every few s, inside zensynora webui)"] -- "due jobs" --> run
    ui -- "Run now" --> run["run_job()<br/>agent.think(prompt)<br/>timeout · retries · clean memory"]
    run --> store
    run -- "post result" --> chan["channel (optional)"]
    run -- "auto-evaluate" --> judge["main model scores 0-10<br/>against success criteria"]
    ui -- "Benchmark" --> bench["same prompt on up to 8 models<br/>time + score side by side"]
    bench --> store
    judge --> store
    tick -- "also" --> ab["automatic backups when due"]

docs.title: 14. Self-update proposals
docs.text:
Added in 0.7.1 (myclaw/selfupdate.py, myclaw/web/medic_api.py, Doctor page, zensynora medic). Agents never write to the program folder.

flowchart TD
    probs["get_recent_problems<br/>log errors · failed / low-score jobs"] --> agent["Agent (medic self-review job,<br/>or any agent you ask in chat)"]
    agent -- read_source_file --> code[("installed code, read-only")]
    agent -- propose_code_change --> check{"inside program folder? no venv/.git/.env?<br/>Python compiles? size ok?"}
    check -- no --> back["refused · reason returned to the agent"]
    check -- yes --> prop["proposal + diff<br/>~/.myclaw/medic/proposals/"]
    prop --> you{"You review<br/>Doctor → Change proposals"}
    you -- reject --> rj["rejected"]
    you -- approve --> stale{"code unchanged<br/>since the proposal?"}
    stale -- no --> outd["failed: ask for a new proposal"]
    stale -- yes --> stage["staging/ = copy of current release + change"]
    stage --> upd["update.sh update --from-dir staging --force<br/>(all steps of §9)"]
    upd -- ok --> ok["new release active · restart to use it ·<br/>zensynora update rollback undoes it"]
    upd -- failure --> rb["rolled back · running version unchanged"]
    agent -- record_lesson --> kb[("knowledge note<br/>medic-lessons")]
    kb -. "found by later searches" .-> agent

docs.title: 15. Telegram bot
docs.text:
myclaw/channels/telegram.py, started by myclaw/web/telegram_api.py (inside zensynora webui) or by myclaw/gateway.py (zensynora gateway). User guide: telegram_guide.md.

Where the bot runs. With channels.telegram.enabled and channels.telegram.run_in_webui (default on) the Web UI process starts the bot. zensynora gateway runs it without the Web UI. Telegram lets only one copy of a bot receive messages: a second copy gets "conflict" and the Web UI stops its own.

flowchart LR
    tgapp(["Telegram app<br/>you, on your phone"]) <--> tgsrv["Telegram servers"]
    subgraph webproc["zensynora webui · one process"]
        tapi["web/telegram_api.py<br/>status · test · restart"]
        tch1["TelegramChannel"]
        reg1["agent registry<br/>same agents as the Web UI"]
        tapi --> tch1 --> reg1
    end
    subgraph gwproc["zensynora gateway · alternative"]
        tch2["TelegramChannel"]
        reg2["agent registry"]
        tch2 --> reg2
    end
    tch1 -- "polling" --> tgsrv
    tch2 -. "polling, only if the Web UI copy is off" .-> tgsrv
    reg1 & reg2 --> kb[("main knowledge base<br/>shared with the Web UI")]
    reg1 & reg2 --> mem[("conversation memory<br/>one per Telegram user")]
    settings["Settings → Channels<br/>Test bot · Restart bot"] --> tapi

One message, end to end.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as You in Telegram
    participant T as Telegram servers
    participant C as TelegramChannel
    participant Q as Queue
    participant W as Worker
    participant A as Agent
    U->>T: "@writer a haiku about rain"
    T->>C: update via polling
    C->>C: allowFrom check: numeric id or @username
    alt not allowed
        C-->>C: log the user id once and ignore
    else allowed
        C->>Q: put the message
        Q->>W: next message of this chat
        Note over Q,W: several workers, so several chats in parallel,<br/>one message at a time per chat
        W->>T: typing… while the agent works
        W->>W: @agent routing: remove @YourBot,<br/>match @writer ignoring case, else default agent
        W->>A: think(text) with this user's memory
        A-->>W: answer, or a short plain error
        W->>W: split into messages of at most 4096 characters
        W->>T: send each part, as plain text if Markdown fails
        T-->>U: answer
    end
  • /start, /help and /whoami answer everyone; all other commands need an allowed user.
  • Photos, voice messages and documents: the caption is used as the message; without a caption the bot says it can only read text for now.
  • Agents created later (create_agent, Settings) are found without a restart.
  • Answers from a named agent start with @Name:.
  • Polling is the default; zensynora gateway --webhook-url … --port 8443 switches the gateway copy to webhook mode (path /webhook). The Web UI copy always polls. ZENSYNORA_TELEGRAM_API_URL points either copy at a self-hosted Bot API server.

Diagrams are Mermaid; GitHub renders them directly. Standalone dark-theme pages are generated into diagrams/ with python diagrams/generate.py.

docs.title: 16. Providers, keys and agents
docs.text:
Since the Unreleased changes a provider can hold several named API keys (providers.<name>.keys; the plain api_key is the Default key). Each agent, the default model and every rotation entry pick a provider, a key and a model. With providers.<name>.rotate_keys on, a rate-limited or exhausted key makes the agent try the same model with the provider's other keys before the next model. Cooldowns are kept per provider, model and key.

flowchart LR
    agent["Agent<br/>provider · key · model"] --> pick{"key id"}
    pick -- "empty" --> defkey["Default key<br/>providers.X.api_key"]
    pick -- "work" --> named["Named key<br/>providers.X.keys[work]"]
    pick -- "unknown" --> warn["warning in the log<br/>uses the Default key"] --> defkey
    defkey & named --> client["provider client<br/>cached per provider + key"]
    client --> llm(["model server"])
    llm -- "429 · quota · 401" --> rot{"rotate_keys on?"}
    rot -- "yes" --> other["same model,<br/>next key of the provider"] --> client
    rot -- "no" --> next["next model in the rotation list"]

docs.title: ZenSynora Backends Guide
docs.text: Applies to: v0.7.0 · Reviewed: 2026-10-13. Commands use the installed zensynora CLI (python cli.py … from the source folder is equivalent).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ZenSynora supports multiple terminal backends for execution across different environments:

  • Local - Direct shell execution on local system
  • Docker - Execution within Docker containers
  • SSH - Remote execution via SSH connection
  • WSL2 - Linux execution via WSL2

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class AbstractBackend {
        <<abstract>>
        +execute(command, timeout)
        +upload(local_path, remote_path)
        +download(remote_path, local_path)
        +get_type()
        +is_available()
    }
    class LocalBackend
    class DockerBackend
    class SSHBackend
    class WSL2Backend

    AbstractBackend <|-- LocalBackend
    AbstractBackend <|-- DockerBackend
    AbstractBackend <|-- SSHBackend
    AbstractBackend <|-- WSL2Backend

    class BackendDiscovery {
        +discover_backends()
        +get_default_backend()
    }

docs.title: Backend Discovery
docs.text:
from myclaw.backends.discover import discover_backends, get_default_backend

# Discover all available backends
available = discover_backends()
for backend in available:
    print(f"Available: {backend.get_type()}")

# Get default backend
default = get_default_backend()
print(f"Default: {default.get_type()}")

docs.title: Using a Specific Backend
docs.text:
from myclaw.backends import LocalBackend, DockerBackend, SSHBackend, WSL2Backend

# Local execution
local = LocalBackend()
result = await local.execute("ls -la")

# Docker execution
docker = DockerBackend({"container": "zensynora"})
result = await docker.execute("python script.py")

# SSH execution
ssh = SSHBackend({"host": "server.com", "user": "admin", "key_path": "~/.ssh/id_rsa"})
result = await ssh.execute("ls")

# WSL2 execution
wsl2 = WSL2Backend()
result = await wsl2.execute("ls /home")

docs.title: config.py
docs.text:
backends = {
    "default_backend": "local",
    "docker": {
        "container": "zensynora",
        "image": "zensynora:latest"
    },
    "ssh": {
        "host": "",
        "user": "",
        "port": 22,
        "key_path": ""
    },
    "wsl2": {
        "distro": "Ubuntu"
    }
}

docs.title: LocalBackend
docs.text:
Direct shell execution on the local system.

Requirements: - Python 3.9+ - Shell (bash/powershell)

Features: - Fast execution - No network required - Access to local filesystem

docs.title: DockerBackend
docs.text:
Execution within Docker containers.

Requirements: - Docker installed - Docker daemon running

Configuration: 

docker_config = {
    "container": "zensynora",
    "image": "zensynora:latest",
    "network": "bridge"
}

docs.title: SSHBackend
docs.text:
Remote execution via SSH.

Requirements: - SSH server access - SSH key or password

Configuration: 

ssh_config = {
    "host": "server.com",
    "user": "admin",
    "port": 22,
    "key_path": "~/.ssh/id_rsa"
}

docs.title: WSL2Backend
docs.text:
Linux execution via WSL2.

Requirements: - WSL2 installed - Python in WSL2

Configuration: 

wsl2_config = {
    "distro": "Ubuntu",  # WSL2 distribution name
    "python_path": "python3"  # Python executable in WSL2
}

docs.title: AbstractBackend
docs.text:
class AbstractBackend:
    def __init__(self, config: dict = None)
    async def execute(command: str, timeout: int = 30) -> Tuple[str, int]
    async def upload(local_path: str, remote_path: str) -> bool
    async def download(remote_path: str, local_path: str) -> bool
    def get_type() -> str
    def is_available() -> bool
    def get_info() -> dict

docs.title: BackendRegistry
docs.text:
class BackendRegistry:
    @classmethod
    def register(backend: AbstractBackend) -> None
    @classmethod
    def get_all() -> List[AbstractBackend]
    @classmethod
    def get_available() -> List[AbstractBackend]
    @classmethod
    def get_by_type(backend_type: str) -> Optional[AbstractBackend]
    @classmethod
    @classmethod
    def clear() -> None

docs.title: Backend not available
docs.text:
Cause: Required software not installed.

Solution: Install Docker/WSL2/configure SSH as needed.

docs.title: Connection timeout
docs.text:
Cause: Network issue or server unreachable.

Solution: Check network connectivity and server status.

docs.title: Permission denied
docs.text:
Cause: Insufficient permissions.

Solution: Check file permissions and SSH key access.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use local for development - Faster iteration
  2. Use Docker for consistency - Reproducible environments
  3. Use SSH for remote servers - Access remote resources
  4. Use WSL2 for Linux tools - Best of both worlds

Generated: 2026-03-29 Part of: ZenSynora Phase 4 Implementation

docs.title: ZenSynora Personal — Recommended LLM Configuration
docs.text:
Variant: Personal (local-first, solo user, privacy-focused) Date: 2026-04-20 Goal: Pick the right local model for your hardware and use case.

Updated 2026-10-13 (v0.7.0). Model advice below is from April 2026; the setup notes in this box are current.

  • Any provider works the same way. Choose it in Web UI → Settings → Model, click Test connection & list models, pick a model, save. No restart needed.
  • llama.cpp (llama-server) — provider llamacpp, URL http://localhost:8080/v1 (or wherever you run it). Start it with --jinja so agents can use tools; without it ZenSynora still chats but retries without tools.
  • Ollama — provider ollama, URL http://localhost:11434. The configured model must be pulled (ollama pull …), otherwise Ollama answers 404.
  • LM Studio — provider lmstudio, URL http://localhost:1234/v1.
  • zensynora doctor tells you whether the server is reachable and whether the configured model exists on it.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
For the Personal variant, the ideal LLM depends on your hardware. ZenSynora is agent-heavy (tool calling, multi-step reasoning, knowledge RAG, swarm coordination), so tool-use reliability and context-window size matter more than raw chat quality.

Hardware Profile Recommended Model Size VRAM Needed Speed* Best For High-end GPU Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct 32B ~22 GB (Q4) ~25 t/s Power user: complex swarms, large KB RAG Mid-range GPU Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct 14B ~10 GB (Q4) ~45 t/s Sweet spot: excellent tools, fast, affordable Entry GPU Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 7B ~5 GB (Q4) ~75 t/s Budget builds, basic agent tasks CPU-only Llama 3.2 3B 3B ~2 GB (Q4) ~8 t/s Minimal hardware, offline-only mode

* Tokens per second on typical consumer hardware. Measured with Ollama, Q4_K_M quantization.

docs.title: Why Qwen2.5 for ZenSynora?
docs.text:
ZenSynora's Personal variant performs these LLM-intensive operations:

  1. Parallel tool calling (agent.py lines 1200–1300) — The LLM must emit valid JSON tool calls, often multiple at once.
  2. Knowledge RAG — Context windows include system prompt + memory history + KB search results (can exceed 8K tokens).
  3. Swarm coordination — The orchestrator sends aggregated outputs back to the LLM for synthesis.
  4. Medic / NewTech analysis — Long-form reasoning over logs, code diffs, and news articles.

Qwen2.5 outperforms Llama 3.x and Mistral on function-calling benchmarks (BFCL, Nexus) while maintaining strong reasoning scores. Its 128K context window handles large RAG retrievals without truncation.

Model Tool-Use Score (BFCL) MATH Reasoning Context ZenSynora Fit Qwen2.5-14B 89.2 79.1 128K ⭐ Best balance Llama 3.3-70B 84.5 83.2 128K Great, needs more VRAM Mistral-Small-3-24B 82.1 81.5 128K Good alternative Qwen2.5-32B 91.5 85.3 128K Best quality, more VRAM Llama 3.2-3B 61.0 52.0 128K Current default — limited

docs.title: Tier 1: High-End Workstation (RTX 4090 / 48GB+ VRAM)
docs.text:
Model: qwen2.5:32b (Q4_K_M) VRAM: ~22 GB Speed: ~25 tokens/s Use Case: Heavy swarm work, large knowledge bases (10K+ notes), coding assistance.

# Ollama setup
ollama pull qwen2.5:32b

# ZenSynora config (~/.myclaw/config.json)
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "provider": "ollama",
      "model": "qwen2.5:32b"
    }
  }
}

Why this tier: The 32B parameter count handles complex multi-hop reasoning (e.g., "Analyze this error log, check the knowledge base for similar issues, propose a fix, and validate it with the Medic agent").

docs.title: Tier 2: Mid-Range Gaming GPU (RTX 3060 12GB / RTX 4060 Ti 16GB / RX 6800 XT)
docs.text:
Model: qwen2.5:14b (Q4_K_M) — Recommended default for most users VRAM: ~10 GB Speed: ~45 tokens/s Use Case: Daily driver — chat, knowledge search, tool execution, light swarm work.

ollama pull qwen2.5:14b

Config: 

{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "provider": "ollama",
      "model": "qwen2.5:14b"
    }
  }
}

Performance expectation: - Simple chat response: 1–2 seconds - Tool call + execution + response: 3–5 seconds - Knowledge RAG with 20 retrieved notes: 4–6 seconds - 3-agent swarm synthesis: 8–12 seconds

This is the sweet spot — 14B is the smallest model that reliably handles parallel tool calls and follows complex system prompts.

docs.title: Tier 3: Entry GPU (RTX 3050 6GB / GTX 1660 Ti 6GB / Integrated GPU)
docs.text:
Model: qwen2.5:7b (Q4_K_M) VRAM: ~5 GB Speed: ~75 tokens/s Use Case: Basic chat, single-tool calls, small knowledge base.

ollama pull qwen2.5:7b

Trade-offs: - Tool calling is reliable for single tools, but parallel multi-tool execution may hallucinate or skip steps. - Reasoning depth is adequate for simple Q&A but struggles with 3+ step planning. - Recommend keeping memory.summarization_threshold low (e.g., 10 messages) to preserve context.

docs.title: Tier 4: CPU-Only / Low-Power Laptop (No discrete GPU)
docs.text:
Model: llama3.2:3b (current default) VRAM/RAM: ~2 GB Speed: ~8 tokens/s (Apple M3: ~25 t/s) Use Case: Offline fallback, quick queries, simple shell commands.

ollama pull llama3.2:3b

Caveats: - Knowledge gap handling (agent.py lines 1000–1100) will trigger more often because the 3B model has weaker recall. - Complex swarms should be limited to 2 agents max. - Consider using cloud APIs (OpenAI/Groq) as a fallback for hard tasks by setting up dual providers.

docs.title: Alternative Models Worth Considering
docs.text: Model When to Choose It Llama 3.3 70B If you have 48GB VRAM and want the best open-source reasoning. Slightly worse tool-use than Qwen2.5-32B but stronger on coding benchmarks. Mistral Small 3 (24B) If you want a European/Apache-2.0 model. Excellent context handling, very strong at 128K RAG tasks. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B If your workflow is reasoning-heavy (math, code debugging, Medic agent log analysis). Slower due to chain-of-thought output, but higher accuracy. Phi-4 (14B) If you need a compact model with surprisingly strong reasoning. Good for laptops with 16GB unified memory (Apple Silicon). Command R (35B) If you primarily do knowledge-base RAG. Built for retrieval-augmented generation with excellent citation accuracy.

docs.title: Context Window Budget for ZenSynora
docs.text:
ZenSynora's agent.py builds a context window from:

Component Typical Size Notes System prompt 500–1,500 tokens Agent personality + available tools schema Memory history 2,000–6,000 tokens Last N messages (configurable) Knowledge RAG 1,000–4,000 tokens Top-K retrieved notes Tool results 500–3,000 tokens Shell output, web browse content User message 50–500 tokens Current query Total ~4,000–15,000 tokens 128K context is overkill but safe

Recommendation: Even the 7B model's 128K window is sufficient. The bottleneck is not context length — it's the model's ability to pay attention to the right parts of that context. Qwen2.5 models handle this well.

docs.title: Ollama Tuning for ZenSynora
docs.text:
Create a custom Modelfile to optimize for agentic behavior:

FROM qwen2.5:14b

# Lower temperature for more deterministic tool calls
PARAMETER temperature 0.3

# Higher repeat penalty to avoid loops (important for Agent.think())
PARAMETER repeat_penalty 1.15

# Slightly higher top-p for creative synthesis tasks
PARAMETER top_p 0.9

# System prompt tuned for tool use
SYSTEM """You are ZenSynora, a helpful AI assistant with access to tools.
When a user asks a question, first determine if a tool is needed.
If multiple tools are independent, call them in parallel.
Always respond in the user's language. Be concise but thorough."""

ollama create zensynora-agent -f ./Modelfile

Then set model: "zensynora-agent" in config.

docs.title: Dual-Provider Fallback Strategy
docs.text:
For CPU-only users or when local models struggle, configure a cloud fallback:

{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "provider": "ollama",
      "model": "qwen2.5:14b"
    }
  },
  "providers": {
    "groq": {
      "api_key": "YOUR_GROQ_KEY",
      "enabled": true
    }
  },
  "intelligence": {
    "routing": {
      "enabled": true,
      "allowed_models": ["qwen2.5:14b", "llama3-70b-8192"],
      "allowed_providers": ["ollama", "groq"]
    }
  }
}

ZenSynora's IntelligentRouter (backends/router.py) can automatically fall back to Groq's llama3-70b-8192 when: - Local Ollama is unreachable - The query is flagged as complex (coding, math, multi-step) - The user explicitly prefixes with /cloud

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Your Setup Recommended Model One-Liner RTX 4090 / 48GB+ qwen2.5:32b Maximum capability for heavy agent work RTX 3060 12GB / 4060 Ti qwen2.5:14b Best value — the daily driver GTX 1660 / 3050 qwen2.5:7b Fast and capable for basic tasks No GPU / laptop llama3.2:3b Minimal, but consider cloud fallback Apple M3/M4 Pro qwen2.5:14b or phi4 Excellent unified memory performance

Bottom line: Start with qwen2.5:14b. It is the best-balanced open model for agentic workloads as of early 2026, and it runs comfortably on the most common consumer GPU (12–16 GB VRAM).

Generated: 2026-04-20

docs.title: Medic & Doctor Guide
docs.text:
Applies to: v0.7.1 · Rewritten: 2026-10-13 · v0.7.1: self-update proposals and learning (section 6) Before 0.7.0 most medic tools described here did not exist in the code (two "health" tools returned fixed text). Everything below is implemented and covered by tests/test_doctor_medic.py.

The doctor checks your installation and tells you how to fix what's wrong. The medic agent gives the AI agents the same checks as tools, plus file-integrity protection, recovery, code validation and a guard against runaway loops.

You want to… Use Check everything from a terminal zensynora doctor See the same report in the browser Web UI → Doctor Repair safe things automatically zensynora doctor --fix or Fix automatically Get one file to understand or share a problem zensynora doctor --report or Doctor → Report → Download Let an agent check/repair itself the medic tools below (available to every agent) Let agents propose fixes to the code (you approve) Doctor → Change proposals, zensynora medic (section 6)

docs.title: 1. The doctor
docs.text:
zensynora doctor              # full report
zensynora doctor --problems   # only warnings and failures
zensynora doctor --offline    # skip the model-server checks
zensynora doctor --fix        # apply safe fixes, then re-check
zensynora doctor --json       # machine-readable
zensynora doctor --report     # diagnostics report → ./zensynora-report-YYYYmmdd-HHMM.md
zensynora doctor --report ~/r.json   # .json, or .zip (report + log tail); --hours 168 = 7 days

Exit code: 0 healthy, 1 warnings, 2 failures — handy for scripts and monitoring.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Category Check Auto-fix environment Python ≥ 3.11 · running inside the venv · required packages · provider libraries (e.g. openai for llama.cpp) · free disk · RAM · CPU load — configuration config file exists and matches the schema · providers known · API keys present for cloud providers · Telegram bot: token set, someone allowed, where it runs (Telegram guide) — llm (network) default model server reachable (latency) · configured model is offered by the server — data ~/.myclaw writable, standard folders present · every SQLite database passes PRAGMA quick_check · data migrations up to date · knowledge index (see below) · chat channels (see below) folders, migrations, knowledge sync security config.json, .config_key, audit secret and update backups are owner-only · Web UI access mode permissions install version, managed vs. legacy layout, updater present · Web UI built — runtime errors and repeated warnings in ~/.myclaw/logs/zensynora.log in the last 24 h · restarts (crash loop) · systemd service state — integrity installed code matches the recorded hash baseline —

Safe fixes never delete anything: they create missing folders, tighten file permissions (600/700), run pending data migrations and sync the knowledge index.

Checks that look for trouble a running install collects:

Check (id) Warning / failure when… What to do Restarts (restart_loop) more than 10 starts of the service (gateway / webui) in 15 minutes. Failure if it is still happening, warning if it happened earlier in the last 24 h. Short commands like zensynora doctor do not count. sudo systemctl status myclaw, journalctl -u myclaw -n 100 — the errors in the report are usually the cause Errors in the last 24 h (recent_errors) any ERROR or CRITICAL line, or a WARNING seen 5 times or more. Messages that differ only in numbers or ids count as one kind (task_webui_123 and task_webui_456). Failure with 3 or more CRITICAL lines. Doctor → Report → Errors shows each kind with its log lines and traceback Custom tools (custom_tools) an enabled tool in ~/.myclaw/TOOLBOX holds placeholder credentials (YOUR_…_HERE, YOUR_BOT_TOKEN, "xxx", <token>) or a hard-coded secret (Telegram token, sk-… key) disable it (disable_skill, or "enabled": false in toolbox_registry.json) and use the built-in tools, e.g. send_telegram_message Knowledge index (knowledge_index) 3 or more note files (or more than 10 %) are not in the index, or the full-text index of note text is missing zensynora knowledge sync or zensynora doctor --fix Agent skills (skills) an agent lists a skill that does not exist, or a SKILL.md of yours is unreadable or empty Skills page, or Settings → Agents MCP servers (mcp_servers) a configured server's command is not installed (not on PATH) install it (Node.js for npx, uv for uvx) or fix the command Chat channels (chat_db) answers left unfinished by a stop, or channel members that are no longer agents restart the Web UI — it repairs both at start

All of them read local files only and take well under a second.

docs.title: Diagnostics report
docs.text:
zensynora doctor --report [PATH] (or Web UI → Doctor → Report) writes one file with everything needed to understand a problem:

  • all doctor checks with hints;
  • warnings and errors of the period, grouped (count, first/last time, module, message) with up to a few raw log lines and tracebacks each;
  • restarts (how many, most in 15 minutes, typical gap);
  • failed, timed-out or interrupted job runs, open change proposals, number of medic lessons;
  • system (OS, Python, CPU, RAM, disk) and installation (folders, release);
  • a configuration summary — which providers have a key, agents with provider and model, channels on/off — never the keys or tokens themselves;
  • the last 200 log lines.

Anything in log text that looks like a token, API key or password (Telegram tokens, sk-…, AIza…, Bearer …, api_key=…, passwords in URLs) is replaced by [redacted]. Formats: Markdown (default), .json, and .zip (report.md + report.json + zensynora.log.tail.txt). API: GET /api/doctor/report, GET /api/doctor/report/download?format=md|json|zip&hours=24, GET /api/doctor/errors?hours=24&level=ERROR&q=text.

docs.title: Adding a check
docs.text:
Checks live in myclaw/doctor/checks.py. One function per check:

from .registry import OK, WARN, FAIL, check, fixer

@check("ollama_models", "Ollama has at least one model", "llm", network=True)
def _ollama_models(ctx):
    ...
    return WARN, "no models pulled", "Run: ollama pull llama3.2"

@fixer("ollama_models")          # optional, only for safe repairs
def _fix(ctx):
    ...
    return "pulled llama3.2"

Return (status, detail, hint). A check that raises is reported as a failure instead of breaking the report.

docs.title: 2. Medic tools (for agents)
docs.text:
All tools are registered in myclaw/tools/__init__.py and implemented in myclaw/agents/medic_agent.py.

Tool What it does check_system_health(offline=False) One-line verdict plus every warning/failure from the doctor get_health_report(offline=False, as_json=False) Full doctor report check_memory_usage(threshold_percent=85) RAM usage, warns above the threshold scan_files(file_paths="") Record SHA-256 hashes of the installed code as the integrity baseline verify_file_integrity(file_path="") Report files modified or missing since the baseline enable_hash_check(enabled=True) Turn integrity checking on/off create_backup(file_path) / list_backups() Copy a file to ~/.myclaw/medic/backups/ / list copies recover_file(file_path, allow_main=False) Restore a file — see below detect_errors_in_file(file_path) Syntax check for .py, .json, .yaml, .toml validate_modification(file_path, new_content) Check a proposed change before writing it: syntax, size, risky calls (eval, os.system, shell=True …) check_file_virustotal(file_path, api_key="") Look up the file's SHA-256 on VirusTotal (the file is not uploaded) record_task_execution(task_name, success, duration_seconds, error) Log a task outcome get_task_analytics(days=7) Success rate, average duration, most-failing tasks prevent_infinite_loop(record=True) Runaway-loop guard status (see below) read_source_file(path, start_line, max_lines) / list_source_files(pattern) Read the installed code (read-only; never venv/, .git, .env) — v0.7.1 propose_code_change(title, reason, file_path, new_content, files_json) File a change proposal; installed only after you approve it — v0.7.1 list_change_proposals(status) Proposals and their status — v0.7.1 get_recent_problems(hours=24) Grouped log errors (incl. CRITICAL), repeated warnings, restarts / crash loop, risky custom tools, failed or low-scoring job runs, open proposals — v0.7.1 record_lesson(topic, lesson) Save a lesson to the knowledge note medic-lessons — v0.7.1

docs.title: Integrity and recovery
docs.text:
• The doctor records a baseline automatically the first time it runs and after every update (a new version means new reference files).
  • verify_file_integrity compares the installed files with it.
  • recover_file restores a file only inside the installation folder (paths like ../../etc/passwd are refused). It first saves a copy of the current (possibly damaged) file, then restores:
  • the local backup whose hash matches the baseline (the known-good copy), otherwise the newest local backup;
  • otherwise the file from GitHub at the tag v<installed version>;
  • from the latest main only if you pass allow_main=True.

For a whole broken installation, zensynora update rollback or zensynora update --force is the better tool (UPDATING.md).

docs.title: Runaway-loop guard
docs.text: The agent router calls prevent_infinite_loop() on every processing step. If more than medic.max_loop_iterations steps (default 100) happen within one minute, further processing is refused until the rate drops — protection against an agent that keeps calling tools or delegating forever. Before 0.7.0 this guard imported a function that did not exist and never triggered.

docs.title: 3. Configuration
docs.text:
~/.myclaw/config.json → medic (also editable in Web UI → Settings for the commonly used keys):

Key Default Meaning enabled false Enables the startup scan in the gateway scan_on_startup false Run the doctor when zensynora gateway starts enable_hash_check true Integrity checking on/off (tool enable_hash_check overrides it) max_loop_iterations 100 Steps per minute before the loop guard blocks repo_url https://github.com/adrianx26/zensynora Source for recover_file from GitHub backup_dir "" Custom folder for file backups (default ~/.myclaw/medic/backups) virustotal_api_key "" Needed by check_file_virustotal

Files written by the medic: ~/.myclaw/medic/integrity.json (baseline), state.json (hash-check override), tasks.jsonl (analytics), backups/.

Logs: since 0.7.0 ZenSynora writes a rotating JSON log to ~/.myclaw/logs/zensynora.log (10 MB × 5). Set MYCLAW_LOG_FILE=off to disable it, or MYCLAW_LOG_FILE=/path/file.log to move it.

docs.title: 4. Log analysis, evolution and change management
docs.text:
The deeper medic modules are Python APIs (not LLM tools):

  • myclaw/agents/medic_evolver.py — deterministic log analysis: pattern and cascade detection, a 0–100 health score and prioritised recommendations (analyze_logs, generate_evolution_proposal).
  • myclaw/agents/medic_change_mgmt.py — change plans with approval, rollback steps, audit log, scheduled reviews and continuous monitoring (create_change_plan, approve_change, execute_change, analyze_system_logs, start_continuous_monitoring, …). Its log analyzer now reads ~/.myclaw/logs/zensynora.log (before 0.7.0 no log file was written, so it never found anything).

Details: MEDIC_CHANGE_MGMT.md.

docs.title: 5. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause / fix LLM server reachable: cannot reach … Start your model server (llama.cpp, Ollama…) and check the URL in Settings → Model. LLM provider libraries: llamacpp needs 'openai' zensynora update --force (or pip install openai in the venv). Configuration file: invalid The config doesn't match the schema; restore the last backup: zensynora update status → zensynora update restore --backup NAME. Databases: … malformed Restore your data from an update backup (same commands). Code integrity: N file(s) differ If you didn't edit them, use recover_file or zensynora update --force. Loop guard blocks normal use Raise medic.max_loop_iterations. The chat says "the model … returned an empty answer twice" The model server answered with nothing (overloaded free tier, a reasoning model that ran out of tokens, a model without tool support). Try again, pick another model on the Models page, or turn on rotation there. Errors in the last 24 h … no such column: write Fixed in 0.7.1 (knowledge search parsed text as FTS5 syntax). Update with zensynora update. Delegation answers "Agent registry not initialized" Fixed in 0.7.1. Update with zensynora update.

docs.title: 6. Self-update proposals
docs.text:
Added in v0.7.1 · code: myclaw/selfupdate.py · tests: tests/test_selfupdate.py

Agents can improve ZenSynora's own code — but never by writing to the program folder. They propose; you decide; the safe updater installs.

flowchart LR
    agent["Agent / medic self-review"] -- read_source_file --> code[("installed code<br/>read-only")]
    agent -- propose_code_change --> prop["Proposal<br/>~/.myclaw/medic/proposals/"]
    prop -- checks --> chk{"inside program folder?<br/>Python compiles?<br/>size ok?"}
    chk -- no --> rej["refused, reason told to the agent"]
    chk -- yes --> you{"You: Doctor → Change proposals<br/>or zensynora medic approve"}
    you -- reject --> done1["rejected"]
    you -- approve --> stage["copy of current release<br/>+ the change"]
    stage --> upd["safe updater<br/>backup · build · verify · switch"]
    upd -- ok --> applied["new release active<br/>(restart ZenSynora)"]
    upd -- failure --> rb["automatic rollback<br/>running version unchanged"]

How a proposal is checked. Paths must stay inside the installed program folder; venv/, .git, node_modules, build output, .env and the config key are off limits; Python files must compile; at most 20 files of 400 KB each; a unified diff is stored for review. Changes that touch only .md, .txt or .rst files are low risk; everything else is high risk.

How it is installed. On approval, the current release is copied (without venv/), the change is applied to the copy, and update.sh update --from-dir <copy> --force runs — full data and program-folder backup, side-by-side build, checks against your settings (and the test suite when medic.self_update.run_tests is on), switch, automatic rollback on any failure. If a file changed after the proposal was made, the install is refused ("ask for a new proposal"). The result and the updater log are kept with the proposal. Undo an installed change with zensynora update rollback.

Commands.

zensynora medic proposals [--status pending]
zensynora medic show ID          # reason + diff
zensynora medic approve ID       # approve and install now
zensynora medic reject ID --note "not needed"
zensynora medic apply ID         # install an approved one / retry a failed one
zensynora medic problems         # what the medic looks at

Settings (Settings → Features → Self-update by agents, or config.json):

Setting Default Meaning medic.self_update.enabled true Agents may read the code and file proposals medic.self_update.auto_approve_low_risk false Install documentation-only proposals without asking medic.self_update.run_tests false Run the test suite on the new release before switching (needs pytest in the venv)

Self-update needs the standard install (~/.local/share/zensynora, made by install-online.sh or zensynora update). Docker and portable installs can still review proposals but install them by rebuilding / copying.

docs.title: Learning
docs.text:
• get_recent_problems groups identical errors from the log and lists failed or low-scoring job runs (score below 6) and open proposals.
  • record_lesson appends to the knowledge note medic-lessons, so every agent can find past causes and fixes with a normal knowledge search; the Doctor page lists them.
  • Run self-review (Doctor page) — or the Medic self-review job template, e.g. daily at 03:00 — asks the default agent to look at the problems, read the code involved, propose at most one small fix and record what it learned. The run is scored like any job, so the Jobs page shows how useful the reviews are. Other agents can join through the chat (for example @coder review proposal …) and by delegation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting (v0.7.2)
docs.text: Symptom Cause / fix The Web UI still shows the old version after zensynora update The old server is still running. Stop it (Ctrl+C), start zensynora webui again (from 0.7.2 on, an old terminal switches to the new version by itself) and reload the page. The chat shows {"tool": "…", "args": …} as the answer The model writes tool calls as text. Fixed in 0.7.2 — such calls now run. A job or chat ends with "[Error] … only available to specific apps" OpenRouter refuses that model for ZenSynora. Pick another model; use Test on the Models page. (v0.7.3) "[Error] … rate-limited" Free models are often busy. Wait a minute or turn on rotation with a second model. (v0.7.3) LM Studio answers nothing / "Unexpected endpoint" Load a model in LM Studio; the URL needs /v1 (added automatically since 0.7.3). A job ends with "I needed more tool steps" Raise the job's Tool steps (default 8), or name the website in the prompt. 🩺 Ask the medic on the run suggests both. (v0.7.5) A job keeps failing and you don't know why 🩺 Ask the medic on the failed run (Jobs page), or set the job's When a run fails to diagnose or fix. (v0.7.5) A channel member can't be removed / no agent can be added ("Unknown agent") An agent was renamed or deleted. Fixed in 0.7.5: open the Web UI once and the channel is repaired.

docs.title: ZenSynora New Tech Agent Guide
docs.text: Applies to: v0.7.0 · Reviewed: 2026-10-13. Commands use the installed zensynora CLI (python cli.py … from the source folder is equivalent).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The New Tech Agent monitors AI news and generates technology implementation proposals. It helps identify emerging technologies that could benefit ZenSynora.

Note: This agent requires explicit user opt-in consent.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.9+
  • ZenSynora core installed
  • Network access (for news fetching)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Add to your config.py:

newtech = {
    "enabled": True,
    "interval_hours": 24,
    "share_consent": True,
    "github_repo_owner": "YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME",
    "github_repo_name": "zensynora",
    "github_token": "ghp_xxx",
    "max_news_items": 10
}

Important: Set share_consent: True only if you want proposals shared on GitHub.

docs.title: GitHub Issue Configuration
docs.text:
share_proposal(..., format="issue") now requires both repository fields:

  • newtech.github_repo_owner
  • newtech.github_repo_name

If either field is missing, issue creation fails gracefully with a clear error message while Gist sharing continues to work unchanged.

Cause: Network issue or all sources failed.

Solution: Check internet connection. Results may be cached.

docs.title: Scheduler Reliability Layer (Phase 6.3)
docs.text:
Applies to: v0.7.0 · Reviewed: 2026-10-13. Commands use the installed zensynora CLI (python cli.py … from the source folder is equivalent).

Adds six capabilities to AsyncScheduler and the schedule tool family:

# Capability Module / API 1 Automatic output validation OutputValidator (built-ins below) 2 Retry + fallback for failed jobs RetryPolicy(max_attempts, backoff, fallback) 3 Automatic task complexity evaluation ComplexityAnalyzer.analyze(task) 4 Auto-splitting complex tasks decompose_task(task) / auto_schedule() 5 Spawn sub-tasks from inside a job JobContext.spawn_subtask(...) 6 Checkpointing + progress reporting Checkpoint + JobContext.progress(...) 7 Smart time allocation per task TaskBudget.from_complexity(...)

All additions are opt-in: existing add_job() callers and existing job functions continue to work unchanged. New behaviour is activated only when you pass the corresponding kwargs.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• myclaw/scheduler_features.py — building blocks (RetryPolicy, ComplexityAnalyzer, decompose_task, Checkpoint, TaskBudget, JobContext, validators)
  • myclaw/async_scheduler.py — Job carries the new fields; _execute_job runs through _run_with_reliability
  • myclaw/tools/scheduler.py — agent-callable tools: auto_schedule, estimate_complexity, get_checkpoint, list_checkpoints, clear_checkpoint
  • tests/test_scheduler_features.py — 37 unit + integration tests

docs.title: 1 · Output validation
docs.text:
from myclaw.scheduler_features import NotEmpty, Regex, JSONSchema, Chain
from myclaw.async_scheduler import AsyncScheduler

scheduler.add_job(
    fetch_summary, "interval", hours=1,
    validator=Chain((NotEmpty(), Regex(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}"))),
)

A validator returns None on success, an error string on failure. Built-ins:

  • NotEmpty() — non-empty result
  • Regex(pattern) — regex match against str(result)
  • MaxLength(n) — bounded result size
  • JSONSchema(required_keys=(...), types={...}) — lightweight, no jsonschema dep
  • Custom(predicate, description="...") — wrap any bool predicate
  • Chain((v1, v2, ...)) — short-circuiting AND

A validation failure raises ValidationError internally, which counts as a retryable failure (so it triggers the RetryPolicy if one is set).

docs.title: 2 · Retry + fallback
docs.text:
from myclaw.scheduler_features import RetryPolicy

def fallback(job, exc, ctx):
    log.error("job %s gave up: %s", job.id, exc)
    notify_oncall(job.id)

scheduler.add_job(
    flaky_job, "date", run_date=now,
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(
        max_attempts=5,
        backoff="exponential",  # "fixed" | "linear" | "exponential"
        base_delay=2.0,
        max_delay=60.0,
        retry_on=(IOError, TimeoutError, ValidationError),
        fallback=fallback,
    ),
)
  • Backoff is capped at max_delay.
  • retry_on defaults to (Exception,).
  • The fallback callable receives (job, last_exc, ctx) and may be sync or async. Its return value is propagated as the job result.
  • Non-retryable exceptions skip remaining attempts and go straight to fallback.

docs.title: 3 · Complexity evaluation
docs.text:
from myclaw.scheduler_features import ComplexityAnalyzer

c = ComplexityAnalyzer.analyze(
    "Browse the news site, summarize headlines, then email the digest"
)
# ComplexityScore(score=0.62, estimated_tool_calls=8,
#                 estimated_duration_s=85.0, detected_steps=3,
#                 flags=['complex', 'slow-ops', 'multi-step', 'decomposition-recommended'],
#                 decompose=True)

Heuristics counted: slow-op keywords (browse, scrape, search, analyz…, compile, research, …), multi-step keywords (then, and, after, next, finally, …), explicit numbered/bullet lists, raw length, mentions of known tool names.

Agent-facing wrapper:

from myclaw.tools import estimate_complexity
print(estimate_complexity("..."))  # JSON

docs.title: 4 · Auto-decomposition
docs.text:
from myclaw.scheduler_features import decompose_task

decompose_task("1. pull repo\n2. run tests\n3. publish report")
# ["pull repo", "run tests", "publish report"]

Decomposition strategy (first match wins): 1. Numbered list (1. … 2. …) 2. Bullet list (- … - …) 3. Multi-step keyword split (then, and then, , followed by, ;) 4. Single task → return as-is

Agent-facing wrapper:

from myclaw.tools import auto_schedule

auto_schedule(
    "1. fetch data\n2. transform\n3. publish",
    delay=60, user_id="u42",
)
# 📊 Complexity: 0.71 (complex, multi-step, explicit-list, decomposition-recommended)
#    Estimated: 6 tool calls · ~52s · 3 step(s)
# 🪓 Auto-split into 3 sub-task(s):
#    • auto_u42_…_sub0: fetch data
#    • auto_u42_…_sub1: transform
#    • auto_u42_…_sub2: publish

auto_schedule(..., auto_split=False) skips decomposition.

docs.title: 5 · Spawn sub-tasks from inside a running job
docs.text:
A job function opts in by declaring a ctx (or context) kwarg:

from myclaw.scheduler_features import JobContext

async def parent(ctx: JobContext = None):
    ctx.progress("phase-1: planning", 1, 3)
    plan = make_plan()
    ctx.progress("phase-2: spawning workers", 2, 3, plan=len(plan))

    for i, item in enumerate(plan):
        ctx.spawn_subtask(child_job, item, sub_id=f"worker-{i}")

    ctx.progress("phase-3: parent done", 3, 3)

Sub-tasks are scheduled on the same AsyncScheduler with a date trigger, so they run once. ctx.spawned returns the list of child IDs.

The scheduler injects ctx only if the job function declares a parameter named ctx, context, or job_ctx. Existing functions without that parameter are unaffected.

docs.title: 6 · Checkpointing + progress reporting
docs.text:
scheduler.add_job(my_job, "date", run_date=now, checkpoint_enabled=True)

Inside the job:

async def my_job(ctx: JobContext = None):
    ctx.progress("step-1", 1, 4, fetched=120)
    ...
    ctx.progress("step-2", 2, 4)
    ...

Each progress() call appends to ~/.myclaw/checkpoints/<job_id>.json:

{
  "task_id": "my_job",
  "status": "completed",
  "last_step": "step-4",
  "last_update": "2026-05-05T17:42:01+00:00",
  "data": {"fetched": 120, "step_n": 4, "step_total": 4},
  "history": [
    {"step": "attempt_1_start", "at": "...", "status": "in_progress"},
    {"step": "step-1", "at": "...", "status": "in_progress"},
    {"step": "step-2", "at": "...", "status": "in_progress"},
    {"step": "step-3", "at": "...", "status": "in_progress"},
    {"step": "step-4", "at": "...", "status": "in_progress"},
    {"step": "completed", "at": "...", "status": "completed"}
  ],
  "total_steps": 4,
  "progress": 1.0
}

The scheduler also writes checkpoints automatically at attempt start, on retry, on validation failure, on timeout, and on fallback.

Agent-facing inspection tools:

from myclaw.tools import get_checkpoint, list_checkpoints, clear_checkpoint

list_checkpoints()         # JSON array of all jobs with checkpoints
get_checkpoint("job_id")   # full state JSON
clear_checkpoint("job_id") # delete the file

Note — checkpoints record progress; they do not yet support resume-from-step. A crash mid-job still requires the job to start over. Resume is a future extension.

docs.title: 7 · Smart time allocation
docs.text:
from myclaw.scheduler_features import ComplexityAnalyzer, TaskBudget

c = ComplexityAnalyzer.analyze(task_string)
budget = TaskBudget.from_complexity(c, multiplier=1.5, floor_s=60, ceiling_s=1800)

scheduler.add_job(my_job, "date", run_date=now, budget=budget)

budget.duration_s becomes a wall-clock timeout enforced by asyncio.wait_for. A TimeoutError triggers retry if RetryPolicy(retry_on=...) includes it (which the default (Exception,) does).

Inside the job, ctx.elapsed(), ctx.remaining_budget(), ctx.is_over_soft_budget() (default 70 %), and ctx.is_over_budget() let the job adapt:

async def adaptive(ctx: JobContext = None):
    while work_remaining():
        if ctx.is_over_soft_budget():
            ctx.progress("soft-budget hit; checkpointing partial result")
            return partial_result()
        do_work_chunk()

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime
from myclaw.async_scheduler import AsyncScheduler
from myclaw.scheduler_features import (
    ComplexityAnalyzer, RetryPolicy, TaskBudget,
    Chain, NotEmpty, JSONSchema,
)

task_text = "1. fetch latest CVEs\n2. correlate with installed packages\n3. write report"
c = ComplexityAnalyzer.analyze(task_text)

scheduler.add_job(
    run_security_audit,
    "interval", hours=6,
    id="sec-audit",
    complexity=c,
    budget=TaskBudget.from_complexity(c),
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, backoff="exponential", base_delay=5.0),
    validator=Chain((NotEmpty(), JSONSchema(required_keys=("cves", "matches")))),
    checkpoint_enabled=True,
)

That single call gives you: validated output, automatic retry with exponential backoff, a duration budget derived from task complexity, and a JSON checkpoint trail for every run.

docs.title: Web scraping
docs.text: Applies to: v0.7.0 · Reviewed: 2026-10-13. Commands use the installed zensynora CLI (python cli.py … from the source folder is equivalent). Scrapling is installed with the core requirements; its browsers are installed by install.sh / the updater (scrapling install).

docs.title: Scrapling
docs.text:
Scrapling is an adaptive Web Scraping framework that handles everything from a single request to a full-scale crawl.

Its parser learns from website changes and automatically relocates your elements when pages update. Its fetchers bypass anti-bot systems like Cloudflare Turnstile out of the box. And its spider framework lets you scale up to concurrent, multi-session crawls with pause/resume and automatic proxy rotation — all in a few lines of Python. One library, zero compromises.

Blazing fast crawls with real-time stats and streaming. Built by Web Scrapers for Web Scrapers and regular users, there's something for everyone.

Requires: Python 3.10+

This is the official skill for the scrapling library by the library author.

docs.title: Setup (once)
docs.text:
Create and activate a virtual Python environment first, then install Scrapling inside that environment:

python -m pip install "scrapling[all]>=0.4.2"

Then do this to download all the browsers' dependencies:

scrapling install --force

Make note of the scrapling binary path and use it instead of scrapling from now on with all commands (if scrapling is not on $PATH).

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Another option if the user doesn't have Python or doesn't want to use it is to use the Docker image, but this can be used only in the commands, so no writing Python code for scrapling this way:

docker pull pyd4vinci/scrapling
or 
docker pull ghcr.io/d4vinci/scrapling:latest

docs.title: CLI Usage
docs.text:
The scrapling extract command group lets you download and extract content from websites directly without writing any code.

Usage: scrapling extract [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Commands:
  get             Perform a GET request and save the content to a file.
  post            Perform a POST request and save the content to a file.
  put             Perform a PUT request and save the content to a file.
  delete          Perform a DELETE request and save the content to a file.
  fetch           Use a browser to fetch content with browser automation and flexible options.
  stealthy-fetch  Use a stealthy browser to fetch content with advanced stealth features.

docs.title: Usage pattern
docs.text:
• Choose your output format by changing the file extension. Here are some examples for the scrapling extract get command:
  • Convert the HTML content to Markdown, then save it to the file (great for documentation): scrapling extract get "https://blog.example.com" article.md
  • Save the HTML content as it is to the file: scrapling extract get "https://example.com" page.html
  • Save a clean version of the text content of the webpage to the file: scrapling extract get "https://example.com" content.txt
  • Output to a temp file, read it back, then clean up.
  • All commands can use CSS selectors to extract specific parts of the page through --css-selector or -s.

Which command to use generally: - Use get with simple websites, blogs, or news articles. - Use fetch with modern web apps, or sites with dynamic content. - Use stealthy-fetch with protected sites, Cloudflare, or anti-bot systems.

When unsure, start with get. If it fails or returns empty content, escalate to fetch, then stealthy-fetch. The speed of fetch and stealthy-fetch is nearly the same, so you are not sacrificing anything.

docs.title: Key options (requests)
docs.text:
Those options are shared between the 4 HTTP request commands:

Option Input type Description -H, --headers TEXT HTTP headers in format "Key: Value" (can be used multiple times) --cookies TEXT Cookies string in format "name1=value1; name2=value2" --timeout INTEGER Request timeout in seconds (default: 30) --proxy TEXT Proxy URL in format "http://username:password@host:port" -s, --css-selector TEXT CSS selector to extract specific content from the page. It returns all matches. -p, --params TEXT Query parameters in format "key=value" (can be used multiple times) --follow-redirects / --no-follow-redirects None Whether to follow redirects (default: True) --verify / --no-verify None Whether to verify SSL certificates (default: True) --impersonate TEXT Browser to impersonate. Can be a single browser (e.g., Chrome) or a comma-separated list for random selection (e.g., Chrome, Firefox, Safari). --stealthy-headers / --no-stealthy-headers None Use stealthy browser headers (default: True)

Options shared between post and put only:

Option Input type Description -d, --data TEXT Form data to include in the request body (as string, ex: "param1=value1&param2=value2") -j, --json TEXT JSON data to include in the request body (as string)

Examples:

# Basic download
scrapling extract get "https://news.site.com" news.md

# Download with custom timeout
scrapling extract get "https://example.com" content.txt --timeout 60

# Extract only specific content using CSS selectors
scrapling extract get "https://blog.example.com" articles.md --css-selector "article"

# Send a request with cookies
scrapling extract get "https://scrapling.requestcatcher.com" content.md --cookies "session=abc123; user=john"

# Add user agent
scrapling extract get "https://api.site.com" data.json -H "User-Agent: MyBot 1.0"

# Add multiple headers
scrapling extract get "https://site.com" page.html -H "Accept: text/html" -H "Accept-Language: en-US"

docs.title: Key options (browsers)
docs.text:
Both (fetch / stealthy-fetch) share options:

Option Input type Description --headless / --no-headless None Run browser in headless mode (default: True) --disable-resources / --enable-resources None Drop unnecessary resources for speed boost (default: False) --network-idle / --no-network-idle None Wait for network idle (default: False) --real-chrome / --no-real-chrome None If you have a Chrome browser installed on your device, enable this, and the Fetcher will launch an instance of your browser and use it. (default: False) --timeout INTEGER Timeout in milliseconds (default: 30000) --wait INTEGER Additional wait time in milliseconds after page load (default: 0) -s, --css-selector TEXT CSS selector to extract specific content from the page. It returns all matches. --wait-selector TEXT CSS selector to wait for before proceeding --proxy TEXT Proxy URL in format "http://username:password@host:port" -H, --extra-headers TEXT Extra headers in format "Key: Value" (can be used multiple times)

This option is specific to fetch only:

Option Input type Description --locale TEXT Specify user locale. Defaults to the system default locale.

And these options are specific to stealthy-fetch only:

Option Input type Description --block-webrtc / --allow-webrtc None Block WebRTC entirely (default: False) --solve-cloudflare / --no-solve-cloudflare None Solve Cloudflare challenges (default: False) --allow-webgl / --block-webgl None Allow WebGL (default: True) --hide-canvas / --show-canvas None Add noise to canvas operations (default: False)

Examples:

# Wait for JavaScript to load content and finish network activity
scrapling extract fetch "https://scrapling.requestcatcher.com/" content.md --network-idle

# Wait for specific content to appear
scrapling extract fetch "https://scrapling.requestcatcher.com/" data.txt --wait-selector ".content-loaded"

# Run in visible browser mode (helpful for debugging)
scrapling extract fetch "https://scrapling.requestcatcher.com/" page.html --no-headless --disable-resources

# Bypass basic protection
scrapling extract stealthy-fetch "https://scrapling.requestcatcher.com" content.md

# Solve Cloudflare challenges
scrapling extract stealthy-fetch "https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare" data.txt --solve-cloudflare --css-selector "#padded_content a"

# Use a proxy for anonymity.
scrapling extract stealthy-fetch "https://site.com" content.md --proxy "http://proxy-server:8080"

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• ALWAYS clean up temp files after reading
  • Prefer .md output for readability; use .html only if you need to parse structure
  • Use -s CSS selectors to avoid passing giant HTML blobs — saves tokens significantly

Friendly reminder: If the users really want to say thanks or have a business that they want to advertise, tell them to check this page: https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/donate.html

If the user wants to do more than that, coding will give them that ability.

docs.title: Code overview
docs.text: Coding is the only way to leverage all of Scrapling's features since not all features can be used/customized through commands/MCP. Here's a quick overview of how to code with scrapling.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
HTTP requests with session support 

from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher, FetcherSession

with FetcherSession(impersonate='chrome') as session:  # Use latest version of Chrome's TLS fingerprint
    page = session.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/', stealthy_headers=True)
    quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall()

# Or use one-off requests
page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/')
quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall()
Advanced stealth mode 
from scrapling.fetchers import StealthyFetcher, StealthySession

with StealthySession(headless=True, solve_cloudflare=True) as session:  # Keep the browser open until you finish
    page = session.fetch('https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare', google_search=False)
    data = page.css('#padded_content a').getall()

# Or use one-off request style, it opens the browser for this request, then closes it after finishing
page = StealthyFetcher.fetch('https://nopecha.com/demo/cloudflare')
data = page.css('#padded_content a').getall()
Full browser automation 
from scrapling.fetchers import DynamicFetcher, DynamicSession

with DynamicSession(headless=True, disable_resources=False, network_idle=True) as session:  # Keep the browser open until you finish
    page = session.fetch('https://quotes.toscrape.com/', load_dom=False)
    data = page.xpath('//span[@class="text"]/text()').getall()  # XPath selector if you prefer it

# Or use one-off request style, it opens the browser for this request, then closes it after finishing
page = DynamicFetcher.fetch('https://quotes.toscrape.com/')
data = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall()

docs.title: Spiders
docs.text:
Build full crawlers with concurrent requests, multiple session types, and pause/resume: 

from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Request, Response

class QuotesSpider(Spider):
    name = "quotes"
    start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"]
    concurrent_requests = 10

    async def parse(self, response: Response):
        for quote in response.css('.quote'):
            yield {
                "text": quote.css('.text::text').get(),
                "author": quote.css('.author::text').get(),
            }

        next_page = response.css('.next a')
        if next_page:
            yield response.follow(next_page[0].attrib['href'])

result = QuotesSpider().start()
print(f"Scraped {len(result.items)} quotes")
result.items.to_json("quotes.json")
Use multiple session types in a single spider: 
from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Request, Response
from scrapling.fetchers import FetcherSession, AsyncStealthySession

class MultiSessionSpider(Spider):
    name = "multi"
    start_urls = ["https://example.com/"]

    def configure_sessions(self, manager):
        manager.add("fast", FetcherSession(impersonate="chrome"))
        manager.add("stealth", AsyncStealthySession(headless=True), lazy=True)

    async def parse(self, response: Response):
        for link in response.css('a::attr(href)').getall():
            # Route protected pages through the stealth session
            if "protected" in link:
                yield Request(link, sid="stealth")
            else:
                yield Request(link, sid="fast", callback=self.parse)  # explicit callback
Pause and resume long crawls with checkpoints by running the spider like this: 
QuotesSpider(crawldir="./crawl_data").start()
Press Ctrl+C to pause gracefully — progress is saved automatically. Later, when you start the spider again, pass the same crawldir, and it will resume from where it stopped.

docs.title: Advanced Parsing & Navigation
docs.text:
from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher

# Rich element selection and navigation
page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/')

# Get quotes with multiple selection methods
quotes = page.css('.quote')  # CSS selector
quotes = page.xpath('//div[@class="quote"]')  # XPath
quotes = page.find_all('div', {'class': 'quote'})  # BeautifulSoup-style
# Same as
quotes = page.find_all('div', class_='quote')
quotes = page.find_all(['div'], class_='quote')
quotes = page.find_all(class_='quote')  # and so on...
# Find element by text content
quotes = page.find_by_text('quote', tag='div')

# Advanced navigation
quote_text = page.css('.quote')[0].css('.text::text').get()
quote_text = page.css('.quote').css('.text::text').getall()  # Chained selectors
first_quote = page.css('.quote')[0]
author = first_quote.next_sibling.css('.author::text')
parent_container = first_quote.parent

# Element relationships and similarity
similar_elements = first_quote.find_similar()
below_elements = first_quote.below_elements()
You can use the parser right away if you don't want to fetch websites like below: 
from scrapling.parser import Selector

page = Selector("<html>...</html>")
And it works precisely the same way!

docs.title: Async Session Management Examples
docs.text:
import asyncio
from scrapling.fetchers import FetcherSession, AsyncStealthySession, AsyncDynamicSession

async with FetcherSession(http3=True) as session:  # `FetcherSession` is context-aware and can work in both sync/async patterns
    page1 = session.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/')
    page2 = session.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/', impersonate='firefox135')

# Async session usage
async with AsyncStealthySession(max_pages=2) as session:
    tasks = []
    urls = ['https://example.com/page1', 'https://example.com/page2']

    for url in urls:
        task = session.fetch(url)
        tasks.append(task)

    print(session.get_pool_stats())  # Optional - The status of the browser tabs pool (busy/free/error)
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(session.get_pool_stats())

docs.title: References
docs.text:
You already had a good glimpse of what the library can do. Use the references below to dig deeper when needed - references/mcp-server.md — MCP server tools and capabilities - references/parsing — Everything you need for parsing HTML - references/fetching — Everything you need to fetch websites and session persistence - references/spiders — Everything you need to write spiders, proxy rotation, and advanced features. It follows a Scrapy-like format - references/migrating_from_beautifulsoup.md — A quick API comparison between scrapling and Beautifulsoup - https://github.com/D4Vinci/Scrapling/tree/main/docs — Full official docs in Markdown for quick access (use only if current references do not look up-to-date).

This skill encapsulates almost all the published documentation in Markdown, so don't check external sources or search online without the user's permission.

docs.title: Guardrails (Always)
docs.text:
• Only scrape content you're authorized to access.
  • Respect robots.txt and ToS.
  • Add delays (download_delay) for large crawls.
  • Don't bypass paywalls or authentication without permission.
  • Never scrape personal/sensitive data.

docs.title: ZenSynora Skill Adapter Guide
docs.text: Applies to: v0.7.0 · Reviewed: 2026-10-13. Commands use the installed zensynora CLI (python cli.py … from the source folder is equivalent).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Skill Adapter enables ZenSynora to analyze, convert, and integrate skills from external standards (particularly agentskills.io open standard) into the ZenSynora TOOLBOX system.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.9+
  • ZenSynora core installed
  • Network access (for fetching external skills)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Add to your config.py:

SKILL_ADAPTER_ENABLED = True
EXTERNAL_SKILL_SOURCES = ["agentskills.io"]
ALLOW_EXTERNAL_REGISTRATION = True

docs.title: 1. Analyze External Skill
docs.text:
Analyze a skill from URL or file path:

from myclaw.agents.skill_adapter import analyze_external_skill

result = analyze_external_skill(
    skill_url="https://example.com/skill.json",
    style="json"
)
print(result)

Output Example: 

📋 External Skill Analysis

Name: my_custom_skill
Source: agentskills.io
Version: 1.0.0
Description: A skill that does something useful
Tags: utility, automation
Parameters: 2
  - input: str
  - options: dict
Has Implementation: Yes
Convertible: Yes

docs.title: 2. Convert Skill to ZenSynora Format
docs.text:
Convert an external skill to ZenSynora format:

from myclaw.agents.skill_adapter import convert_skill

result = convert_skill(
    skill_source='{"name": "hello_world", "description": "Says hello", "function": "def execute(): return \"Hello!\"", "version": "1.0.0"}',
    target_format="zensynora"
)
print(result)

Output: 

✅ Skill converted successfully!
File: ~/.myclaw/TOOLBOX/hello_world.py
Name: hello_world

docs.title: 3. List Compatible Skills
docs.text:
List all external skills currently in the TOOLBOX:

from myclaw.agents.skill_adapter import list_compatible_skills

result = list_compatible_skills()
print(result)

Output: 

📦 Compatible External Skills:

  • hello_world (v1.0.0) - agentskills.io
  • data_processor (v2.1.0) - external

docs.title: 4. Register External Skill File
docs.text:
Register a Python skill file directly:

from myclaw.agents.skill_adapter import register_external_skill

result = register_external_skill(skill_path="/path/to/skill.py")
print(result)

Output: 

✅ Skill 'skill' registered from /path/to/skill.py

docs.title: JSON Format (agentskills.io)
docs.text:
{
  "name": "skill_name",
  "description": "What the skill does",
  "parameters": [
    {"name": "param1", "type": "string", "required": true},
    {"name": "param2", "type": "int", "required": false}
  ],
  "function": "def execute(param1, param2=''):\n    return f'{param1} {param2}'",
  "tags": ["utility", "automation"],
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "skill_author"
}

docs.title: YAML Format
docs.text:
name: skill_name
description: What the skill does
tags:
  - utility
  - automation
version: 1.0.0
function: |
  def execute(param):
      return f"Result: {param}"

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Ext["External Skill (JSON/YAML)"] --> Parse["parse_external() (Schema Validation)"]
    Parse --> Convert["convert_to_zensynora() (Code Generation)"]
    Convert --> Validate["validate_skill() (AST Compile Check)"]
    Validate --> Register["register_converted() (Save to TOOLBOX)"]

docs.title: Error: Invalid JSON
docs.text:
Cause: The skill source contains invalid JSON.

Solution: Verify the JSON syntax using a JSON validator.

docs.title: Error: File not found
docs.text:
Cause: The specified skill file path doesn't exist.

Solution: Check the file path and ensure the file exists.

docs.title: Error: Invalid Python syntax
docs.text:
Cause: The converted skill contains invalid Python code.

Solution: Manually review the skill function and fix syntax errors.

docs.title: Error: Permission denied
docs.text:
Cause: Cannot write to TOOLBOX directory.

Solution: Check file permissions for ~/.myclaw/TOOLBOX/.
